m01-l01-what-is-electricity.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook
Have you ever felt a tiny shock when touching a doorknob in winter?
That sudden little snap is static electricity jumping through the air.
Electricity powers everything from a wristwatch to an autonomous Mars rover!

<Callout type="safety" title="Safe Lab Practice">
In RoboForge, every hands-on circuit uses low-voltage DC batteries (under 12 volts). Never experiment with household wall sockets or mains power. Wall outlets carry deadly high voltages!
</Callout>

## 2. The Core Idea: What is Charge?
All matter around you is made of tiny atoms.
Atoms contain positive protons and negative electrons.
When electrons are pushed along a conductor like a copper wire, they form an **electric current**.

Think of electric current as water flowing through a closed garden hose.
- **Water particles** are like electric charges.
- **The water pump** acts like a battery pushing the charges.
- **The hose** is the conductive copper wire.

<Callout type="info" title="Where the Water Analogy Breaks">
Water can spill out into the open air from a cut hose. Electric current cannot spill onto your table! Charges will only flow if there is a complete, unbroken closed loop back to the battery.
</Callout>

## 3. See It: A Closed Circuit
To light up a small bulb or an LED, charges must travel in a complete circuit:

1. Electrons start at the negative terminal of the battery.
2. They travel through the connecting wire.
3. They pass through the light bulb, making it glow.
4. They return to the positive terminal of the battery.

If the wire is disconnected at any point, the flow stops instantly.

## 4. Try It Out
Imagine you have a battery, two wires, and an LED bulb.
What happens if you disconnect one wire?
Make your prediction:
- Will the light stay on for a second?
- Or will it turn off immediately?

<Reveal summary="See the explanation">
It turns off immediately! Electric current cannot jump across open air gaps at low voltages. The loop must remain closed.
</Reveal>

## 5. Check Your Understanding
Answer the quiz below to check what you learned.

## 6. Recap
- Electricity is the flow of electric charges through a conductor.
- Current requires a complete, unbroken loop to travel.
- Low-voltage DC batteries provide safe power for our robotics projects.

## 7. What's Next
In the next lesson, we will explore **Voltage, Current, and Resistance**, and see how they work together!

m01-l02-voltage-and-current.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook
Have you ever wondered why a 9V rectangular battery cannot shock you when you touch its terminals with your fingers, but can instantly illuminate an LED or spin a tiny motor? 

The secret lies in the difference between the **electric push** (voltage) and the **charge flow rate** (current).

## 2. Voltage: The Electric Pressure
Voltage (symbol $V$) is measured in **Volts**. Think of voltage as electric pressure created by chemical reactions inside a battery. 

A battery has two terminals:
- **Positive terminal (+)**: High electric potential.
- **Negative terminal (-)**: Low electric potential.

The voltage rating (like $1.5\text{ V}$ for an AA battery or $9\text{ V}$ for a rectangular transistor battery) measures the potential difference between these two poles. The higher the voltage, the harder charges are pushed!

<Callout type="safety" title="Low-Voltage Laboratory Boundary">
In our school robotics curriculum, all battery experiments use safe low-voltage DC power (1.5V to 12V). Human skin has high dry resistance, making voltages under 24V DC completely safe from electrical shock. Never connect anything to AC mains power.
</Callout>

## 3. Current: The Rate of Flow
Current (symbol $I$) is measured in **Amperes** (or **milliamps**, where $1\text{ A} = 1000\text{ mA}$). 

Current tells us how many Coulombs of charge pass through a wire cross-section every single second:
$$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$

In typical robotics circuits:
- A small LED draws about $15\text{ mA}$ to $20\text{ mA}$ ($0.02\text{ A}$).
- A micro servo motor draws about $100\text{ mA}$ to $500\text{ mA}$.
- A tiny digital sensor draws under $5\text{ mA}$.

## 4. Voltage Causes Current
Voltage does not "flow" through a wire — **voltage exists across** two points, and this potential difference causes **current to flow through** the component.

<Callout type="info" title="Think like an Engineer">
You measure **voltage across** a component (in parallel) and **current through** a wire (in series).
</Callout>

## 5. Summary Check
Remember:
1. Voltage is the electrical push ($V$, in Volts).
2. Current is the rate of charge flow ($I$, in Amperes).
3. Current only flows when there is both an electric push (voltage) AND a complete closed circuit path.

m01-l03-resistance-and-ohms-law.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: Why Do We Need Obstacles?
If electric current does useful work (like lighting bulbs and spinning motors), why would we deliberately insert a component whose sole job is to **restrict** current?

Without resistance, an unlimited rush of electrons would surge through delicate semiconductors, overheating battery cells and instantly destroying LEDs! Resistors are the traffic controllers of physical electronics.

## 2. Resistance: Opposing the Flow
Resistance (symbol $R$) measures how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric charges. It is measured in **Ohms** (symbol $\Omega$).
- A thick copper wire has very low resistance (almost $0\,\Omega$).
- A carbon or metal-film resistor has precise resistance (e.g. $220\,\Omega$, $1\,\text{k}\Omega$, $10\,\text{k}\Omega$).
- Air and plastic have immense resistance (billions of Ohms), acting as insulators.

## 3. Ohm's Law: The Fundamental Equation
In 1827, German physicist Georg Ohm discovered that current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance:
$$V = I \times R$$

From this single relationship, we can derive any missing parameter:
- **Find Voltage:** $V = I \times R$
- **Find Current:** $I = \frac{V}{R}$
- **Find Resistance:** $R = \frac{V}{I}$

### Worked Example:
Suppose a $9\text{ V}$ battery powers a circuit with a $300\,\Omega$ resistor. How much current flows?
$$I = \frac{9\text{ V}}{300\,\Omega} = 0.03\text{ A} = 30\text{ mA}$$

<Callout type="safety" title="Component Overheating Rule">
When current flows through a resistor, electrical power is dissipated as heat:
$$P = V \times I$$
Standard small resistors in our robotics kits are rated for $0.25\text{ W}$ (quarter-watt). If you put too much current through a tiny resistor, it will become hot to the touch. Always calculate power before wiring!
</Callout>

## 4. Reading Resistor Color Bands
Most through-hole resistors have 4 colored rings printed around their ceramic body:
1. **Band 1:** First significant digit (e.g., Brown = 1)
2. **Band 2:** Second significant digit (e.g., Black = 0)
3. **Band 3:** Multiplier decade (e.g., Red = $10^2 = 100$)
4. **Band 4:** Tolerance (Gold = $\pm 5\%$)

For example: Brown - Black - Red - Gold represents:
$$10 \times 100 = 1000\,\Omega = 1\,\text{k}\Omega$$

m01-l04-series-circuits.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: One Single Track
Imagine cars driving on a single-lane mountain road with no side exits or detours. Every car that enters must pass through every section of the road in exact sequence. If one bridge collapses, all traffic stops immediately!

This is exactly how a **series circuit** works.

## 2. The Golden Rule of Series Circuits
In a series circuit, components are connected head-to-tail to form a single continuous loop.

Because charge cannot magically appear, disappear, or leak out into the air:
$$\text{The electric current is identical through every component in series!}$$
$$I_{\text{total}} = I_1 = I_2 = I_3$$

## 3. Equivalent Series Resistance
When current passes through multiple resistors in series, it must fight through each obstacle one after another. Therefore, series resistances simply add together:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_n$$

### Example:
If you place a $1000\,\Omega$ resistor and a $2000\,\Omega$ resistor in series:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = 1000 + 2000 = 3000\,\Omega$$

<Callout type="safety" title="Safe Series Resistor Habits">
Always make sure your battery terminals are disconnected before re-arranging series components on your breadboard. A common beginner mistake is accidentally plugging both ends of a wire into the same power rail, creating an accidental battery short circuit!
</Callout>

## 4. Voltage Dividers
While current is the same everywhere in a series loop, the total voltage from the battery splits across each resistor:
$$V_{\text{source}} = V_1 + V_2$$

The voltage dropped across each resistor is directly proportional to its resistance:
$$V_2 = V_{\text{source}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

### Practical Robotics Use:
If a microcontroller pin can only handle $3.3\text{ V}$, but your sensor battery puts out $6.6\text{ V}$, two identical $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ resistors in series create a perfect midpoint $3.3\text{ V}$ tap!

m01-l05-parallel-circuits.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: Independent Branches
You switch off your bedroom lamp. Why does the fan keep spinning?

In homes and robots, components connect in **parallel**. Each device gets its own independent branch.

## 2. Voltage Across Parallel Branches
In parallel circuits, both ends of every part connect to common rails. 

Every parallel branch receives the exact same battery voltage:
$$V_{\text{total}} = V_1 = V_2 = V_3$$

A 9V battery provides 9V to every parallel branch.

## 3. Current Splits at Forks
Charges flow to a junction. The current splits into separate branches. 

Total current equals the sum of branch currents:
$$I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_n$$

Low resistance branches carry more current. High resistance branches carry less.

<Callout type="safety" title="Current Accumulation Hazard">
Parallel branches combine their currents at the battery. Too many branches draw high current. This can overheat small battery cells. Keep total current below 2 Amperes.
</Callout>

## 4. Equivalent Parallel Resistance
Adding parallel branches creates new paths for charges. This lowers overall resistance:
$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$$

For two resistors, use product-over-sum:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{R_1 \times R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

Two equal 1000Ω resistors in parallel yield 500Ω. Parallel paths make current flow easier!

items.explanation: In parallel connections, all components share the same two common nodes, so each branch experiences the full source voltage.

m01-l06-switches-and-buttons.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: Taking Control
So far, circuits operate continuously the moment a battery is connected. But what if you want to turn on a robot headlight only in the dark, or start a motor when a bumper strikes a wall?

Switches provide human and mechanical control over electrical current.

## 2. Opening and Closing the Loop
A switch is simply a mechanical gap controller:
- **Open (OFF):** Metal contacts are physically separated. Air between the contacts has billions of Ohms of resistance, so current stops completely ($I = 0$).
- **Closed (ON):** Metal contacts touch firmly, creating a continuous low-resistance bridge (under $0.05\,\Omega$). Current flows freely.

## 3. Momentary vs Latching
- **Latching Switch:** Stays in its new position after you flip it (like your household light switch or breadboard toggle rocker).
- **Momentary Pushbutton:** Returns to its default state as soon as you release your finger:
  - **Normally Open (NO):** Disconnected by default; pressing closes the connection (like a doorbell or keyboard key).
  - **Normally Closed (NC):** Connected by default; pressing breaks the connection (like an emergency stop button).

<Callout type="safety" title="Emergency Stop Habit">
In mobile robotics and motorized projects, always install a master power switch or accessible battery pull-plug as an emergency stop. If a motor stalls or software crashes, cutting power instantly prevents burned motors and dead batteries.
</Callout>

## 4. Preventing Floating Pins
When connecting a button to a digital microcontroller input (like Arduino Pin 2):
- When the button is pressed, the pin connects firmly to $5\text{ V}$ (HIGH).
- When released, what is the pin connected to? **Nothing!** It is an open floating wire antenna that picks up stray electrostatic noise, causing erratic jumping between 0 and 1!

To solve this, we add a high-value resistor ($10\,\text{k}\Omega$) called a **pull-down resistor** to gently tie the pin to $0\text{ V}$ Ground whenever the button is unpressed.

items.explanation: An unconnected input pin acts like a miniature radio antenna. Pull-up/pull-down resistors ensure a stable default logic level.

m02-l07-diodes-and-leds.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: The One-Way Gate
Have you ever tried pedaling a bicycle backward? The pedals spin freely without moving the wheels. A ratcheting mechanism ensures mechanical force only drives the bicycle forward.

In electronics, **diodes** are electrical one-way valves that allow current to flow in only one direction!

## 2. Polarity: Anode and Cathode
A diode has two terminals:
- **Anode (+)**: Current enters here.
- **Cathode (-)**: Current exits here.

When the anode is more positive than the cathode by at least the **forward voltage drop** ($V_f \approx 0.7\text{ V}$ for silicon, $2.0\text{ V}$ for red LEDs), the diode enters **forward bias** and conducts freely. 

If connected backward (**reverse bias**), the internal barrier widens and blocks current flow entirely!

### How to Identify LED Pins:
- **Longer lead:** Anode (+)
- **Shorter lead / Flat rim on plastic dome:** Cathode (-)

## 3. The Need for Current-Limiting Resistors
Unlike resistors, which have a linear slope ($I = V/R$), LEDs have an exponential curve. Once the forward threshold (approx $2.0\text{ V}$) is exceeded, internal resistance plummets to almost zero.

<Callout type="safety" title="Component Burnout Warning">
If you connect an LED directly across a 5V or 9V battery with no resistor, hundreds of milliamps surge through the microscopic semiconductor die, instantly vaporizing the gold bond wire inside! In real life this produces heat and can pop the plastic lens. Always use a series limiting resistor.
</Callout>

## 4. Calculating the Resistor Value
To calculate the perfect series resistor:
$$R = \frac{V_{\text{source}} - V_{\text{forward}}}{I_{\text{target}}}$$

### Worked Example:
Suppose you power a Red LED ($V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$, $I = 20\text{ mA} = 0.02\text{ A}$) from a $9\text{ V}$ battery:
$$R = \frac{9\text{ V} - 2.0\text{ V}}{0.02\text{ A}} = \frac{7.0\text{ V}}{0.02\text{ A}} = 350\,\Omega$$

A standard, readily available $330\,\Omega$ or $470\,\Omega$ resistor will keep the LED bright, efficient, and completely protected!

m02-l08-capacitors-and-timing.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: The Water Tower Analogy
Have you ever seen a large municipal water tower on a hill? When water pumps pulse intermittently, the reservoir tower cushions the pressure shocks and keeps clean water flowing steadily to home faucets.

In physical circuits, **capacitors** are electrical reservoirs that store charge and cushion voltage fluctuations!

## 2. Anatomy of a Capacitor
A capacitor consists of two conductive plates separated by an insulating material called a **dielectric** (like ceramic, mica, or plastic film).

When connected across a voltage source:
1. Positive charges build up on one plate, while negative electrons accumulate on the other.
2. An electric field forms between the plates, storing potential energy.
3. Once charged to the source voltage, current stops flowing.

Capacitance ($C$) measures charge stored per volt, measured in **Farads** ($F$):
$$1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F} \quad\text{(microfarads)}$$
$$1\,\text{nF} = 10^{-9}\text{ F} \quad\text{(nanofarads)}$$
$$1\,\text{pF} = 10^{-12}\text{ F} \quad\text{(picofarads)}$$

## 3. Polarized vs Ceramic Capacitors
- **Ceramic Disc Capacitors:** Small values ($10\,\text{pF}$ to $100\,\text{nF}$), non-polarized (can be plugged into a breadboard in either orientation).
- **Electrolytic Capacitors:** Large cylindrical cans ($1\,\mu\text{F}$ to $1000\,\mu\text{F}$) with chemical electrolyte. **Strictly polarized!** The negative terminal is marked with a broad white/silver stripe with minus signs (-).

<Callout type="safety" title="Electrolytic Capacitor Polarity Rule">
Never connect an electrolytic capacitor backward or exceed its printed voltage rating (e.g. 16V or 25V). Reverse polarity causes internal gas expansion and can rupture the safety vent on the aluminum can! Always double-check that the striped negative lead connects to 0V Ground.
</Callout>

## 4. The RC Time Constant ($\tau$)
When a capacitor charges through a resistor, it does not fill instantly. The speed of charging depends on both the resistance (choke point) and the capacitance (bucket size):
$$\tau = R \times C$$

- In $1\tau$ (one time constant), the capacitor charges to approx **63.2%** of full voltage.
- In $5\tau$, it reaches **99%** (fully charged).

### Example:
A $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ ($10{,}000\,\Omega$) resistor and a $100\,\mu\text{F}$ ($0.0001\text{ F}$) capacitor:
$$\tau = 10{,}000\,\Omega \times 0.0001\text{ F} = 1.0\text{ second}$$
This predictable delay enables timers, flashers, and debounce filters!

m02-l09-transistors-as-switches.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: The Microscopic Muscle
An Arduino microcontroller's digital output pin can only supply a tiny trickle of current — about $20\text{ mA}$ ($0.02\text{ A}$). If you plug a $500\text{ mA}$ DC robot motor directly into the pin, the chip's internal silicone will burn out immediately.

How can a fragile digital pin control powerful motors, high-intensity lamps, and solenoids? With a **transistor**!

## 2. The NPN Transistor (BJT)
A common NPN transistor (like the classic 2N2222 or 2N3904) has three terminals:
1. **Base (B):** The control gate. Injecting a tiny current here opens the main channel.
2. **Collector (C):** Current enters from the positive load side.
3. **Emitter (E):** Current exits toward 0V Ground.

Think of it like an electrically activated water valve: a child turning a small control wheel (Base current) can open a massive pipeline (Collector current).

## 3. Operating as a Saturated Switch
In digital robotics circuits, we operate the transistor in **saturation** (fully ON):
- When Base voltage is $0\text{ V}$ ($I_B = 0$): The switch is **OPEN** (Cutoff). The load is off.
- When Base voltage is $> 0.7\text{ V}$ ($I_B > 1\text{ mA}$): The switch is **CLOSED** (Saturation). Full battery current flows through the load to Ground!

A current-limiting resistor ($1\,\text{k}\Omega$) is always placed in series with the Base pin to protect the microcontroller.

<Callout type="safety" title="Motor Flyback Voltage Spike Hazard">
DC motors contain coiled copper wire (inductors). When you suddenly switch off a spinning motor, its collapsing magnetic field generates a violent reverse-voltage spike (up to 100V!) that can fry your transistor and microcontroller in a split second. Always place a reverse-biased **flyback diode** (like 1N4001) across the motor terminals to safely dissipate this spike.
</Callout>

## 4. Summary: The Power Multiplier
- Microcontrollers provide logic and brainpower.
- Transistors provide electrical muscle.
- Base resistor protects the controller pin; flyback diode protects against motor inductive kicks.

## 1. Hook: 25 Transistors in a Tiny Black Box
In earlier lessons, we wired single resistors, LEDs, and transistors one by one. But what if you wanted to build an automatic flasher or robot heartbeat generator? Wiring 25 discrete transistors and 15 resistors by hand would fill an entire breadboard!

In 1971, engineer Hans Camenzind etched all of those components onto a piece of silicon smaller than a grain of rice, creating the **NE555 Timer** — the most popular microchip in human history!

## 2. Reading Integrated Circuit Pins
Most hobbyist chips use a **Dual In-line Package (DIP)** with two parallel rows of pins spaced at standard breadboard pitch ($0.1\text{ inches}$ / $2.54\text{ mm}$).

### How to Find Pin 1:
1. Look at the top face of the chip for a **small semicircular notch** or an **embossed circular dot**.
2. Hold the chip so the notch faces upward or left.
3. **Pin 1** is immediately to the left of the notch.
4. Count counter-clockwise around the chip:
   - Pins 1 to 4 go down the left side.
   - Pins 5 to 8 go up the right side.

## 3. The 555 Astable Multivibrator (Heartbeat Mode)
In **astable mode**, the 555 timer oscillates continuously between HIGH ($5\text{ V}$) and LOW ($0\text{ V}$), producing a steady square-wave clock pulse.

- A timing capacitor ($C_1$) slowly charges through resistors $R_1$ and $R_2$.
- When voltage across $C_1$ reaches two-thirds of the supply ($2/3\,V_{cc}$), an internal comparator triggers, driving Output Pin 3 LOW and discharging the capacitor through Pin 7.
- When voltage drops to one-third ($1/3\,V_{cc}$), the output flips back HIGH, repeating the cycle forever!

The oscillation frequency in Hertz is calculated by:
$$f = \frac{1.44}{(R_1 + 2R_2) \times C_1}$$

<Callout type="safety" title="Safe Prototyping Practice">
Integrated circuits are sensitive to static electricity and can heat up if plugged in backward (reversing VCC Pin 8 and GND Pin 1). Always verify the orientation notch before switching on your battery power.
</Callout>

## 4. You Have Mastered Discrete Electronics!
Congratulations! With resistors, diodes, capacitors, transistors, and integrated circuits in your toolkit, you are now ready to progress into programmable embedded microcontrollers (Arduino) and build intelligent autonomous robots!

## 1. Hook: How Does a Robot 'Feel'?
How does your eye sense daylight, or a thermostat detect the cold? They use materials whose physical properties shift when exposed to external energy.

In electronics, **sensors** act as sensory organs. Many fundamental sensors work by changing their electrical resistance!

## 2. Resistive Sensors
Two common examples found in robotics kits:
- **Light Dependent Resistor (LDR / Photoresistor):** Made of cadmium sulfide (CdS). In pitch darkness, resistance exceeds $100\text{ k}\Omega$. Under bright light, photons free electrons, dropping resistance to under $1\text{ k}\Omega$.
- **Thermistor (NTC):** A negative temperature coefficient resistor. As ambient temperature rises, thermal agitation frees carriers and resistance drops.

## 3. The Core Challenge: Measuring Resistance
A microcontroller cannot directly measure resistance. Its analog input pins only measure **voltage** ($0\text{ V}$ to $5\text{ V}$).

How do we turn a changing resistance into a changing voltage? With a **Voltage Divider**!

```
         +5V (Vcc)
           |
          [R1] (e.g. 10k Fixed Resistor)
           |
           +-----> V_out (To Microcontroller Analog Pin)
           |
          [R2] (e.g. LDR Sensor to Ground)
           |
          GND (0V)
```

## 4. The Voltage Divider Equation
When two resistors are placed in series across a voltage source $V_{\text{in}}$, the current through both is:
$$I = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{R_1 + R_2}$$

The voltage dropped across the bottom resistor $R_2$ is:
$$V_{\text{out}} = I \times R_2 = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

### Worked Example:
Assume $V_{\text{in}} = 5\text{ V}$, fixed resistor $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, and an LDR for $R_2$:
1. **In Bright Sunlight ($R_2 = 1\text{ k}\Omega$):**
   $$V_{\text{out}} = 5\text{ V} \times \frac{1\text{ k}\Omega}{10\text{ k}\Omega + 1\text{ k}\Omega} = 5 \times \frac{1}{11} \approx 0.45\text{ V}$$
2. **In Dark Shadow ($R_2 = 90\text{ k}\Omega$):**
   $$V_{\text{out}} = 5\text{ V} \times \frac{90\text{ k}\Omega}{10\text{ k}\Omega + 90\text{ k}\Omega} = 5 \times \frac{90}{100} = 4.5\text{ V}$$

By monitoring $V_{\text{out}}$, our robot instantly knows whether it is in shadow or bright sunlight!

## 5. Summary & Key Takeaways
- Sensors convert environmental stimuli into electrical signals.
- Resistive sensors need a series partner to form a voltage divider.
- Choosing a fixed resistor close to the sensor's mid-range resistance maximizes measurement sensitivity.

## 1. Hook: Rapid Prototyping Without Solder
Before solderless breadboards were invented in the 1970s, engineers wrapped bare wires around brass nails hammered into wooden bread-cutting boards!

Today, solderless breadboards allow you to assemble, test, modify, and disassemble electronic circuits in seconds with zero soldering.

<Callout type="safety" title="Prototyping Safety">
  Always disconnect the battery or USB power cable before inserting or moving jumper wires on a breadboard. Accidentally bridging adjacent rows with power on can cause a short circuit that damages components or overheats wiring. Keep circuit voltage strictly under 12V DC.
</Callout>

## 2. Anatomy of a Solderless Breadboard
If you peel back the adhesive backing of a breadboard, you will find rows of nickel-silver spring clips:
1. **Power Bus Rails (+ and -):**
   - Run along the top and bottom outer edges.
   - Long continuous horizontal strips distributing $+5\text{ V}$ (Red rail) and Ground $0\text{ V}$ (Blue or Black rail).
2. **Terminal Tie-Point Rows (Rows 1 to 30 or 60):**
   - Run vertically in 5-hole groups (A-B-C-D-E and F-G-H-J-K).
   - All 5 holes in a lettered column share one internal metallic clip.
3. **The Center Trough (DIP Divide):**
   - Separates the top half (A-E) from the bottom half (F-K).
   - Designed to straddle Dual In-Line Package (DIP) integrated circuits so opposing IC pins do not short together.

## 3. Switches and Pushbuttons
A switch physically makes or breaks electrical continuity:
- **Latching Switch (Toggle / Slide):** Remains in its new state after being toggled (like a room light switch).
- **Momentary Pushbutton (Tactile Switch):** Only completes the circuit while mechanical pressure is applied, springing open as soon as released.

### The 4-Pin Tactile Button Mystery:
Learners are often confused by 4-pin tactile buttons. Why four pins for a simple switch?
- Pins on the same side across the center trough are internally linked in pairs ($1\leftrightarrow 2$ and $3\leftrightarrow 4$).
- Pressing the button connects pair $(1,2)$ to pair $(3,4)$.
- **Best Practice:** Mount the button straddling the center trough!

## 4. Summary & Prototyping Rules
- Never connect $+5\text{ V}$ and $\text{GND}$ rails together directly.
- Component leads sharing the same 5-hole numbered row are electrically joined.
- Keep jumper wires flat and color-coded: Red for power, Black for ground, Yellow/Green/Blue for signals.

## 1. Hook: The Computer in Your Microwave
When you think of a computer, you likely envision a laptop with high-definition screens, gigabytes of RAM, fans, and an operating system like Windows, macOS, or Linux.

Yet your microwave oven, washing machine, digital wristwatch, and anti-lock brakes also contain computers! How can a $2 chip control a complex machine?

They use a **Microcontroller Unit (MCU)**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Microcontroller Voltage Safety">
  Operate microcontrollers strictly from regulated low-voltage sources (5V USB or 7V–12V DC into the barrel jack). Never short the 5V power pin to GND, and never connect AC mains or batteries exceeding 12V to the board.
</Callout>

## 2. Microprocessor vs Microcontroller
- **Microprocessor (e.g., Intel Core i7, Apple M3):** A pure processing brain (CPU). It requires external RAM chips, SSD storage, power management ICs, and motherboards to operate.
- **Microcontroller (e.g., ATmega328P, ESP32, RP2040):** An entire self-contained computer on a single chip. It contains the CPU, memory, timers, and input/output pins inside one package!

## 3. The Four Pillars of a Microcontroller
1. **CPU (Central Processing Unit):** Fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes mathematical and logical operations.
2. **Flash Memory (ROM):** Non-volatile storage where your compiled program code lives. Stays preserved even when power is turned off! (ATmega328P has $32\text{ KB}$).
3. **SRAM (Static RAM):** Volatile fast memory holding your running variables and call stack. Erased when power is cut! (ATmega328P has $2\text{ KB}$).
4. **GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output):** Physical pins that read electrical voltages from the outside world or assert control signals to LEDs, transistors, and motors.

## 4. The Arduino Uno: A Friendly ATmega328P Carrier
The Arduino Uno is not the microcontroller itself; it is a development board designed to make using the **ATmega328P** chip convenient:
- **16 MHz Crystal Oscillator:** Provides a steady clock heartbeat (16 million cycles per second).
- **5V Voltage Regulator:** Allows powering via 7V–12V DC barrel jack or 5V USB.
- **USB-to-Serial Bridge:** Lets your computer upload code without needing an external programmer.
- **Female Pin Headers:** Allows plugging jumper wires directly without soldering.

## 5. Summary
- Microcontrollers are dedicated computers built for real-time control.
- Code is stored in Flash; variables live in SRAM.
- The Arduino Uno packages the ATmega328P for simple prototyping.

## 1. Beyond 1s and 0s: The Continuous Spectrum
Digital inputs are binary: a light switch is either ON or OFF.

However, the real physical world is continuous and analog:
- A dimmer knob turns gradually from dim to bright.
- A robot battery drains smoothly from $8.4\text{ V}$ down to $6.0\text{ V}$.
- Ambient temperature changes smoothly by fractions of a degree.

To measure these continuous physical states, microcontrollers employ an **Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC)**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Analog Input Voltage Limits">
  The ATmega328P ADC input pins (A0–A5) are designed strictly for 0V to 5V DC signals. Never feed high voltages (such as direct 12V motor battery voltages) into an analog pin without a properly calculated resistive voltage divider to step it down below 5V.
</Callout>

## 2. 10-Bit Resolution & Quantization
The ATmega328P on the Arduino Uno includes a built-in 10-bit Successive Approximation ADC accessible on pins **A0 through A5**.

A 10-bit binary register can represent $2^{10} = 1024$ discrete numbers:
$$\text{Range: } 0 \text{ to } 1023$$

When using the default $5.0\text{ V}$ reference:
- $0.0\text{ V} \rightarrow 0$
- $2.5\text{ V} \rightarrow 512$
- $5.0\text{ V} \rightarrow 1023$

### Voltage Resolution per Step:
$$\text{Step Size} = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{1024} \approx 0.00488\text{ V} = 4.88\text{ mV}$$
The microcontroller can detect voltage variations as tiny as $4.88\text{ millivolts}$!

## 3. Reading a Potentiometer with `analogRead()`
A potentiometer is a 3-terminal adjustable voltage divider:
- Outer pin 1 $\rightarrow 5\text{ V}$
- Outer pin 2 $\rightarrow \text{GND}$
- Center wiper $\rightarrow \text{A0}$

As you turn the knob, the wiper sweeps smoothly between $0\text{ V}$ and $5\text{ V}$.

```cpp
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600); // Initialize serial monitor
}

void loop() {
  int rawValue = analogRead(A0); // Reads 0 to 1023
  float voltage = (rawValue * 5.0) / 1023.0;

  Serial.print("Raw: ");
  Serial.print(rawValue);
  Serial.print(" | Voltage: ");
  Serial.println(voltage);

  delay(200);
}
```

*Note: You do not need to call `pinMode()` for analog input pins; `analogRead()` configures the internal multiplexer automatically.*

## 4. Summary & Practical Tips
- `analogRead()` takes approximately $100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ ($0.0001\text{ s}$) to complete a successive-approximation conversion.
- To convert raw ADC readings to physical units (like temperature, distance, or motor angle), calibrate with a linear mapping equation or lookup curve.

m04-l21-dc-motors-and-back-emf.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: From Sparks to Motion
So far, our circuits have only moved electrons, blinked lights, and computed numbers.

Robotics is about making physical things move in the physical world! The workhorse of robotics motion is the **direct-current (DC) electric motor**.

<Callout type="safety" title="Motor Drive Safety">
  Motors are inductive loads that draw high current. Never power a DC motor directly from an Arduino I/O pin (pins are rated for 20mA max; motors draw 200mA to 800mA). Always use a dedicated battery pack or external supply limited to ≤ 12V DC and ≤ 2A. Never leave a stalled motor powered, as coils can overheat and cause burns.
</Callout>

## 2. How Brushed DC Motors Work
Inside a brushed DC motor:
1. **Permanent Magnets (Stator):** Create a stationary magnetic field.
2. **Coils of Copper Wire (Rotor / Armature):** When electric current passes through the wire, it creates an electromagnet.
3. **Lorentz Force:** Opposite magnetic poles attract and like poles repel, forcing the shaft to rotate.
4. **Commutator & Brushes:** As the shaft turns, mechanical brushes slide across copper contacts, reversing current direction every half-turn to keep rotation continuous.

## 3. Free-Running vs Stall Current
A DC motor has two critical operational states:
- **No-Load Current ($I_{\text{nl}}$):** Motor spins freely in the air without resistance (e.g., $100\text{ mA}$).
- **Stall Current ($I_{\text{stall}}$):** When wheels are locked in place by a heavy load or wall, rotation stops. The motor acts like a dead short circuit of bare copper wire! Current can surge to $800\text{ mA}$ or more, generating intense heat.

## 4. The Inductive Spike Hazard
Motor coils store energy in magnetic fields:
$$E = \frac{1}{2} L \cdot I^2$$

When you turn off a switching transistor, current drops to zero instantly ($dI/dt$ is huge). According to Faraday's law of induction ($V = -L \cdot dI/dt$), the collapsing magnetic field releases its stored energy as a massive high-voltage spike (often exceeding $50\text{ V}$ to $100\text{ V}$)!

This spike instantly punches through the thin silicon junction of your transistor or Arduino chip, destroying it permanently.

## 5. The Solution: The Flyback Diode
Place a rectifier diode (like a `1N4007`) in parallel with the motor terminals, with its cathode pointing toward the positive supply voltage:

```
        +5V / +6V (V_motor)
           |
       +---+---+
       |       |
      [M]     [D] (Flyback Diode: Cathode up)
       |       |
       +---+---+
           |
         [ NPN Transistor or MOSFET Switch ]
           |
          GND
```

When the transistor turns off, the inductive spike circulates harmlessly through the diode loop until its energy dissipates as heat, saving your circuit!

## 6. Summary
- Never drive motors directly from microcontroller pins.
- Budget for stall current, not just running current.
- Always install a flyback diode across inductive motor coils.

## 1. The Reverse Problem
A single transistor switch can turn a motor ON and OFF.

However, to reverse a DC motor, you must reverse the polarity of the voltage applied across its two terminals! How can an autonomous robot reverse without a human manually swapping wires?

The solution is the **H-Bridge**.

<Callout type="safety" title="Motor Driver & Power Safety">
  Always operate mobile robot motor drivers on low voltage (6V to 12V DC battery packs, under 2A). L298N heatsinks can become warm during extended heavy loads; do not touch heatsink surfaces immediately after high-speed runs. Always connect battery negative to Arduino GND to prevent erratic floating gate states.
</Callout>

## 2. The H-Bridge Circuit Architecture
Four electronic switches ($S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$) surround the motor in an "H" configuration:

```
            +V_Motor (+6V to +12V)
               |             |
             [S1]           [S3]
               |             |
               +---[MOTOR]---+
               |             |
             [S2]           [S4]
               |             |
              GND           GND
```

### The Four Operating States:
1. **Forward:** Close $S_1$ and $S_4$. Current flows Left-to-Right through the motor $\rightarrow$ Motor spins Forward.
2. **Reverse:** Close $S_3$ and $S_2$. Current flows Right-to-Left through the motor $\rightarrow$ Motor spins Backward.
3. **Coast (Freewheel):** All switches OPEN ($S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4 = 0$). Current ceases; motor coasts to a gradual stop.
4. **Brake:** Close $S_2$ and $S_4$ (both low-side switches). The motor terminals are shorted together! Rotating momentum generates back-EMF, dynamically fighting rotation and locking the shaft quickly.

## 3. The Deadly "Shoot-Through" Short Circuit
What happens if you accidentally close $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the same time?
Current bypasses the motor entirely, rushing straight from $+V_{\text{motor}}$ to $\text{GND}$ in a dead short circuit! This "shoot-through" condition incinerates driver transistors in milliseconds.

Integrated driver ICs (like the `L298N` and `TB6612FNG`) contain internal lockout logic preventing shoot-through.

## 4. Driving the L298N Module with Arduino
The popular L298N dual H-bridge module has direction inputs (IN1, IN2) and an optional speed enable pin (ENA):

| IN1 | IN2 | Motor Action |
|---|---|---|
| HIGH | LOW | Spin Forward |
| LOW | HIGH | Spin Reverse |
| LOW | LOW | Coast (Stop) |
| HIGH | HIGH | Active Brake |

```cpp
const int IN1 = 5; // Connected to PWM pin for speed control
const int IN2 = 6;

void setMotorSpeed(int speed) {
  if (speed > 0) {
    analogWrite(IN1, speed);
    digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  } else if (speed < 0) {
    digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);
    analogWrite(IN2, -speed);
  } else {
    digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);
    digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  }
}
```

## 5. Summary
- An H-bridge enables full bi-directional motion and active braking.
- Diagonal switch pairs determine polarity.
- Combining PWM on direction inputs provides smooth proportional speed control.

## 1. Hook: Precision Positioning
A DC motor spins continuously. If you turn off power, it coasts to a halt at a random angle.

How can a steering linkage, pan-tilt camera, or robotic arm move to exactly $45^\circ$, stop instantly, and resist external forces trying to push it out of position?

They use **RC Servo Motors**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Servo Power & Mechanical Safety">
  Never power multiple servos from the Arduino board 5V pin. When moving rapidly or loaded, small 9g servos can pull 500mA to 1A each, causing the Arduino regulator to overheat or brown out. Always power servos from an external 5V–6V battery pack (≤ 2A) and connect external Ground to Arduino Ground. Beware of mechanical pinch points.
</Callout>

## 2. Anatomy of a Servo Motor
Inside a compact plastic servo shell (like the classic SG90):
1. **Coreless DC Motor:** High-speed, low-torque miniature motor.
2. **Reduction Geartrain:** Multi-stage nylon or metal gears that sacrifice speed to multiply mechanical torque by over 100 times.
3. **Internal Feedback Potentiometer:** Linked to the output shaft, measuring the physical angle in real time.
4. **Control Circuit Board:** Compares your command signal against the internal potentiometer position. If there is an error, it drives the motor forward or backward until the error reaches zero!

## 3. The 50 Hz Pulse Width Protocol
Servo control is often confused with PWM dimming.

Standard servos do NOT care about the duty cycle percentage. They care strictly about the **absolute pulse width duration**:
- Repeating frame rate: **50 Hz** (one pulse every $20\text{ ms}$).
- **1.0 ms (1000 µs):** Drive to $0^\circ$ (full counter-clockwise).
- **1.5 ms (1500 µs):** Drive to $90^\circ$ (neutral center).
- **2.0 ms (2000 µs):** Drive to $180^\circ$ (full clockwise).

## 4. Servo Wiring (3 Pins)
- **Brown or Black:** Ground ($0\text{ V}$)
- **Red:** Power ($+4.8\text{ V}$ to $+6.0\text{ V}$)
- **Orange, Yellow, or White:** Control signal (PWM GPIO)

## 5. Arduino Servo Code
```cpp
#include <Servo.h>

Servo myServo;

void setup() {
  myServo.attach(9); // Attach to digital pin 9
}

void loop() {
  myServo.write(0);   // Move to 0 degrees
  delay(1000);

  myServo.write(90);  // Center at 90 degrees
  delay(1000);

  myServo.write(180); // Move to 180 degrees
  delay(1000);
}
```

## 6. Summary
- Servos provide closed-loop position control with internal feedback.
- Pulse duration ($1\text{ ms}$ to $2\text{ ms}$) sets the mechanical target angle.
- Always provide dedicated external power with a common ground return.

m04-l24-stepper-motors-basics.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: How Does a 3D Printer Move with Micrometer Precision?
Look at a 3D printer extruding plastic layers thinner than a human hair ($0.1\text{ mm}$). There are no position sensors on the nozzle carriage!

How does the machine know its exact location after four hours of printing?

It uses **Stepper Motors**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Stepper Thermal & Current Safety">
  Unlike DC motors which draw near-zero current at rest, stepper motors draw maximum current when stopped to maintain holding torque! Stepper motor casings can become hot to the touch during normal operation. Always operate with proper driver current-limiting (A4988/TMC2208 VREF) and low-voltage DC supplies ≤ 12V and ≤ 2A.
</Callout>

## 2. Operating Principle: Teeth and Coils
A stepper motor contains:
- **Toothed Permanent Magnet Rotor:** A cylindrical shaft with alternating magnetic teeth.
- **Multi-Phase Stator Coils:** Coils of wire arranged symmetrically around the outer housing.

When electromagnetic Phase A is energized, the rotor's teeth snap into magnetic alignment with Phase A's poles. When Phase B is energized and Phase A de-energized, the rotor snaps forward by one exact angular increment: a **step**!

## 3. Step Angle & Resolution
The smallest angular increment of motion is the **step angle** ($\theta_s$):
$$\text{Steps per Revolution} = \frac{360^\circ}{\theta_s}$$

Common configurations:
- **$1.8^\circ$ Step Angle (NEMA 17 standard):**
  $$\frac{360^\circ}{1.8^\circ} = 200\text{ steps per full revolution}$$
- **$7.5^\circ$ Step Angle (Toy/Can-stack steppers):**
  $$\frac{360^\circ}{7.5^\circ} = 48\text{ steps per full revolution}$$

By commanding exactly 100 electrical pulses, the shaft rotates exactly half a turn ($180^\circ$) without needing any sensor feedback! This is called **open-loop precision**.

## 4. Steppers vs DC Motors vs Servos
| Feature | DC Motor | RC Servo | Stepper Motor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Motion** | Continuous rotation | $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ bounded | Incremental steps ($360^\circ$ continuous) |
| **Feedback** | Open-loop (blind) | Closed-loop (internal pot) | Open-loop (step counting) |
| **Holding Torque** | Zero at rest | Moderate | Very High |
| **Best Application** | Drive wheels, fans | Grippers, steering arms | 3D printers, CNC, robot joints |

## 5. Summary
- Stepper motors convert digital electrical pulses into precise mechanical steps.
- Standard industrial steppers have $200\text{ steps/rev}$ ($1.8^\circ/\text{step}$).
- Steppers draw holding current continuously, keeping joints locked firmly in place.

m04-l25-robot-power-and-current-budgets.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: The Robot That Freezes on Takeoff
You finish assembling your two-wheel autonomous robot car. It sits on your desk, blinking its LEDs happily.

You turn on the drive motors. The wheels twitch forward for a fraction of a second, the robot dies, and the Arduino boots up from the beginning again! Why does the robot reboot every single time the motors start?

You have encountered **Voltage Sag and Brownout**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Battery & Power Safety">
  School-path robotics strictly uses safe low-voltage battery packs (4xAA alkaline or NiMH cells producing 4.8V to 6V DC, ≤ 2A). Never attempt to charge bare Lithium-Polymer (LiPo) or Lithium-Ion pouch cells without specialized balance chargers and dedicated fire-safe enclosures. Disconnect battery packs when leaving the laboratory bench.
</Callout>

## 2. Battery Internal Resistance ($R_{\text{int}}$) & Voltage Sag
A real battery is not an ideal infinite voltage source. It behaves like an ideal voltage source in series with an internal resistance ($R_{\text{int}}$):

$$V_{\text{terminal}} = V_{\text{battery}} - (I_{\text{load}} \times R_{\text{int}})$$

- In resting mode, current is tiny ($50\text{ mA}$): voltage drop is negligible.
- When two TT gearmotors suddenly accelerate, their stall surge current pulls $1.5\text{ A}$!
- The $1.5\text{ A}$ current through $R_{\text{int}}$ causes the battery terminal voltage to plummet from $6.0\text{ V}$ down to $3.5\text{ V}$!
- The Arduino's on-chip Brown-Out Detection (BOD) circuit detects the voltage drop and forces an immediate CPU hardware reset!

## 3. The Power Budget
To design a reliable robot, calculate your maximum and average current requirements:

| Subsystem | Idle Current | Peak / Operating Current |
|---|---|---|
| Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) | $45\text{ mA}$ | $50\text{ mA}$ |
| Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04) | $2\text{ mA}$ | $15\text{ mA}$ |
| Line Tracking IR Modules (x2) | $20\text{ mA}$ | $40\text{ mA}$ |
| Two TT DC Gearmotors | $0\text{ mA}$ | $400\text{ mA}$ (running) / $1400\text{ mA}$ (stall) |
| SG90 Pan Servo | $10\text{ mA}$ | $500\text{ mA}$ (moving) |
| **Total Current Demand** | **$77\text{ mA}$** | **$2005\text{ mA}$ (Peak Peak)** |

Your power supply must be capable of delivering this peak surge current without dropping below the operating voltage threshold.

## 4. The Golden Rule of Robotics: Common Ground
To isolate heavy motor surges from delicate logic chips, roboticists often use **two power sources** (e.g. a USB power bank for the Arduino and a 4xAA battery pack for the motor driver).

When using separate supplies, you **MUST connect their Ground wires together**:
```
  [ Battery 1 (Motors) ]              [ Battery 2 (Logic) ]
       (+)      (-)                        (+)      (-)
        |        |                          |        |
        |        +--------------------------+--------+
        |                    |                       |
   Motors +6V        SHARED COMMON GROUND        Arduino GND (0V)
```
Without a shared common ground, control signals have no reference voltage and float erratically!

## 5. Summary
- Always calculate a full subsystem current budget.
- Account for motor stall surges and battery voltage sag.
- Always bond all power supply negative leads into a shared common ground.

objectives: Understand how slotted optical disc encoders convert mechanical shaft rotation into digital square-wave pulses

keyIdeas: An optical encoder pulses high and low as a slotted wheel breaks an infrared light beam.

m04-l26-rotary-encoders-motion-feedback.rawMarkdown:
## 1. Hook: How Far Did the Robot Drive?
You program your robot to drive forward:
```cpp
setMotors(200, 200);
delay(3000); // Drive for 3 seconds
setMotors(0, 0);
```

Did the robot travel exactly $1.0\text{ meter}$?
- On slick tile, wheels slip and it travels $0.6\text{ m}$.
- On deep carpet, friction slows the wheels and it travels $0.8\text{ m}$.
- As the battery drains, it drives slower each minute.

Open-loop timing cannot measure movement accurately. To navigate reliably, a robot must measure the physical rotation of its wheels using **Rotary Encoders**!

<Callout type="safety" title="Rotating Mechanism Safety">
  When mounting slotted encoder discs to DC gearmotors, verify adequate clearance between the spinning disc and the chassis wall. Keep loose clothing, hair, and fingers away from spinning gears and wheels during testing.
</Callout>

## 2. Optical Slotted Encoders
The simplest encoder consists of:
1. **Slotted Code Wheel:** A black plastic wheel with 20 radial cutouts attached to the motor shaft.
2. **Optocoupler Sensor (Photo-Interrupter):** An infrared LED facing a phototransistor across an optical gap.

As the wheel spins, the solid spokes block the light (Output = LOW) and the slots let light through (Output = HIGH). Each rising edge equals one fractional turn!

### Calculating Distance:
If a wheel has 20 slots ($20\text{ pulses per revolution}$) and a diameter $D = 65\text{ mm}$:
$$\text{Circumference} = \pi \times D = 3.14159 \times 65\text{ mm} \approx 204.2\text{ mm}$$
$$\text{Distance per Pulse} = \frac{204.2\text{ mm}}{20} \approx 10.21\text{ mm per tick}$$

Every time the Arduino detects a pulse, the robot has moved forward by approximately $1\text{ centimeter}$!

## 3. Quadrature Encoding: Detecting Direction
A single sensor counts pulses, but cannot tell if the wheel is spinning **forward** or **backward**!

A **Quadrature Encoder** uses two sensors (Channel A and Channel B) placed out of phase by $90^\circ$ (a quarter-wave):

```
Forward:
Channel A:  ___|---|___|---|___
Channel B:  _____|---|___|---|__  (B lags behind A)

Reverse:
Channel A:  _____|---|___|---|__
Channel B:  ___|---|___|---|___  (B leads ahead of A)
```

By reading the state of Channel B at the exact moment Channel A transitions from LOW to HIGH:
- If B is LOW: Wheel is spinning **Forward**.
- If B is HIGH: Wheel is spinning **Backward**!

## 4. Hardware Interrupts
Because wheels spin fast (often generating hundreds of pulses per second), regular `loop()` code can miss pulses while busy calculating.

Microcontrollers use **Hardware Interrupts** (pins 2 and 3 on the Arduino Uno) that instantly pause normal execution, increment a counter in nanoseconds, and return to the main loop:

```cpp
volatile long pulseCount = 0;

void countPulse() {
  pulseCount++; // Runs instantly in hardware ISR
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);
  // Trigger countPulse() on every rising edge of Pin 2
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), countPulse, RISING);
}
```

## 5. Summary
- Rotary encoders provide closed-loop physical feedback on speed and distance.
- Quadrature phase encoding provides direction and 4x resolution.
- Hardware interrupts ensure no movement ticks are lost during computation.

items.prompt: A robot wheel has a diameter of 60mm and a 20-slot optical encoder disc directly on the wheel axle. How many millimeters does the robot travel per encoder pulse? (Use pi ≈ 3.1416)
items.explanation: Circumference = pi * D = 3.1416 * 60mm = 188.496mm. Distance per pulse = 188.496 / 20 = 9.42mm.

items.prompt: Why are microcontroller hardware interrupts (like attachInterrupt on Arduino pin 2) preferred for encoder counting?

choices.text: They execute immediately in hardware on each pulse edge without missing ticks during CPU loop processing
They reduce the wheel friction
They increase the battery capacity
They eliminate the need for electricity

items.explanation: Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) guarantee that high-speed pulse trains are captured even if the main program is executing other logic.

capacitor-ceramic.name: Ceramic Disc Capacitor (100nF / 0.1µF)
capacitor-ceramic.description: Non-polarized capacitor widely utilized for high-frequency noise filtering, power rail decoupling, and signal coupling across digital ICs.

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Standard 50V DC breakdown rating. Exceeding breakdown causes dielectric punch-through short circuit.

commonMistakes: Placing decoupling capacitor far away from IC power pins; traces introduce parasitic inductance that renders decoupling ineffective.
Expecting large energy storage; 100nF is strictly for high-frequency spikes, not bulk energy storage.
capacitor-ceramic.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Ceramic Capacitor Quick Reference
- **Decoupling Rule:** Place one 100nF (0.1µF) ceramic capacitor as close as physically possible to the VCC and GND pins of every digital IC.
- **Marking Code '104':** 1st digit = 1, 2nd digit = 0, 3rd digit = 4 zeros in picofarads $\to 100,000\,\text{pF} = 100\,\text{nF} = 0.1\,\mu\text{F}$.
- **Non-Polarized:** Can be inserted into breadboard in either direction.
capacitor-ceramic.safetyNotes: Safe for low-voltage school robotics circuits. Do not connect to mains AC voltages or high-voltage circuits.

capacitor-electrolytic.name: Aluminum Electrolytic Capacitor (100µF 25V)
capacitor-electrolytic.description: Polarized capacitor providing high capacitance density, essential for low-frequency power supply filtering, smoothing rectified DC, and decoupling motor current surges.

pinout.name: Cathode (-)
pinout.description: Negative terminal (shorter lead with white stripe on can)

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Strictly polarized. Reverse voltage exceeding 1.5V will cause internal gas buildup and rupture.

commonMistakes: Reverse polarization (connecting negative stripe to positive rail) causes rapid heating, electrolyte venting, or pop.
Exceeding rated breakdown voltage (e.g. connecting a 16V capacitor to a 24V supply).
capacitor-electrolytic.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Electrolytic Capacitor Quick Reference
- **Polarity Identification:** The negative (-) lead is marked by a prominent stripe down the side of the cylindrical can and has a shorter physical wire lead.
- **Voltage De-rating:** Always choose a capacitor rated for at least $1.5\times$ to $2\times$ the maximum expected operating DC voltage.
- **RC Time Constant:** $\tau = R \times C$ (seconds). Full charge requires $\approx 5\tau$.
capacitor-electrolytic.safetyNotes: Never reverse polarity on electrolytic capacitors. In reverse bias, electrolysis generates hydrogen gas causing catastrophic casing rupture.

diode-1n4007.name: 1N4007 1A Power Rectifier Diode
diode-1n4007.description: Standard silicon rectifier diode capable of handling 1.0A continuous forward current and up to 1000V reverse voltage, essential for inductive flyback suppression across motors, relays, and solenoids.

pinout.name: Cathode
pinout.description: Negative terminal marked by silver band

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Continuous forward current limit is 1.0 A. Peak non-repetitive surge current limit is 30 A (8.3 ms half-sine).

commonMistakes: Connecting flyback diode in forward bias across motor supply, creating a dead short across the power rails!
Using for high-frequency switching power supplies (> 20 kHz); standard recovery time (30 µs) creates excessive switching losses.
diode-1n4007.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 1N4007 Flyback Quick Reference
- **Flyback Configuration:** Connect cathode (silver band) to positive motor rail ($V_{\text{motor}}$) and anode to the switched ground (transistor/MOSFET drain/collector).
- **Why Flyback Protection?** When a motor or relay coil is switched OFF abruptly, the collapsing magnetic field produces an inductive voltage spike: $V = -L \frac{di}{dt}$. Without a diode, this spike (often $> 100\,\text{V}$) destroys the switching transistor instantly.
diode-1n4007.safetyNotes: Always install a flyback diode antiparallel across DC inductive loads (motors, solenoids, relays) to protect microcontrollers and driving transistors from inductive flyback spikes.

diode-1n4148.name: 1N4148 Fast Switching Signal Diode
diode-1n4148.description: Ultra-fast silicon epitaxial planar diode with 4ns reverse recovery time, designed for high-frequency signal rectification, wave shaping, and logic gate level protection.

pinout.name: Cathode
pinout.description: Marked by a black stripe on the glass body

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Continuous forward current limit is 200-300 mA. Surge current limit 1.0 A for 1 second.

commonMistakes: Using 1N4148 as a flyback diode for large DC motors (current draw > 300mA); it will overheat and burn out. Use 1N4007 or Schottky for motors.
Reversing cathode and anode due to small glass body markings.
diode-1n4148.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 1N4148 Quick Reference
- **Forward Voltage Drop ($V_f$):** Typically $0.65\,\text{V}$ at $10\,\text{mA}$, rises to $\approx 1.0\,\text{V}$ at $100\,\text{mA}$.
- **Reverse Recovery Time ($t_{rr}$):** $\le 4\,\text{ns}$ (ideal for fast digital logic and microcontroller inputs).
- **Cathode Marking:** The black printed band indicates the cathode (point of the schematic triangle where bar sits).
diode-1n4148.safetyNotes: Rated for small signal processing ($\le 200\,\text{mA}$). Do not use for high-current power supply rectification.

driver-l298n.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### L298N Direction & Speed Truth Table
| ENA (PWM) | IN1 | IN2 | Motor A Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| HIGH / 255 | HIGH | LOW | Forward full speed |
| HIGH / 255 | LOW | HIGH | Reverse full speed |
| PWM (0-255)| HIGH | LOW | Forward at variable speed |

ic-lm358.name: LM358 Dual Operational Amplifier
ic-lm358.description: Industry-standard dual operational amplifier designed for single-supply operation (3V to 32V) with ground-sensing input stages. Used for analog sensor pre-amplification, active filtering, and voltage comparison.

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Differential input voltage limit is 32V. Output short-circuit to ground is continuous.

commonMistakes: Expecting rail-to-rail output swing on VCC side; standard LM358 output can only swing up to $\approx VCC - 1.5\,\text{V}$. On a 5V supply, max output is $\approx 3.5\,\text{V}$.
Leaving the unused op-amp inputs floating; causes oscillations and increased current draw. Wire unused op-amp as a voltage follower connected to ground or mid-rail.
ic-lm358.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### LM358 Basic Op-Amp Configurations
- **Non-Inverting Amplifier:** Gain $A_v = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_{in}}$, $V_{out} = V_{in} \times \left(1 + \frac{R_f}{R_{in}}\right)$.
- **Inverting Amplifier:** Gain $A_v = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}$, $V_{out} = -V_{in} \times \frac{R_f}{R_{in}}$.
- **Voltage Follower (Buffer):** Connect Pin 1 (1OUT) directly to Pin 2 (1IN-). Input on Pin 3 (1IN+). Provides high input impedance ($> 10\,\text{M}\Omega$) and low output impedance.
- **Comparator:** Connect sensor signal to Pin 3 and reference threshold to Pin 2. Output saturates to HIGH or LOW.
ic-lm358.safetyNotes: LM358 input common-mode range includes Ground (0V), making it well-suited for single-supply 5V Arduino circuits.

ic-ne555.name: NE555 Precision Timer IC
ic-ne555.description: Legendary 8-pin mixed-signal timer IC configured in astable mode (free-running square wave oscillator) or monostable mode (one-shot pulse generator). Can source or sink up to 200mA directly.

pinout.name: TRIG
pinout.description: Trigger input, starts timing cycle when voltage drops below 1/3 VCC

pinout.name: OUT
pinout.description: High-current push-pull output stage (sources or sinks up to 200 mA)

pinout.name: RESET
pinout.description: Active-LOW reset; connect directly to VCC if unused

pinout.name: CTRL
pinout.description: Control voltage (2/3 VCC); bypass with 10nF capacitor to GND for noise immunity

pinout.name: THRES
pinout.description: Threshold input, resets flip-flop when voltage rises above 2/3 VCC

pinout.name: DISCH
pinout.description: Open-collector discharge pin connected to internal NPN transistor

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Maximum supply voltage VCC is 18V. Output sink/source limit is 200 mA.

commonMistakes: Leaving Pin 4 (RESET) floating; random electro-static noise will reset the internal flip-flop erratically. Always tie Pin 4 to Pin 8 (VCC) if not actively driving it.
Omitting the 100nF decoupling capacitor across Pin 1 and Pin 8; during output switching, the push-pull output creates a transient supply rail glitch.
ic-ne555.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### NE555 Astable Mode Formulas
- **Charge Time (HIGH):** $t_{\text{high}} = 0.693 \times (R_A + R_B) \times C$
- **Discharge Time (LOW):** $t_{\text{low}} = 0.693 \times R_B \times C$
- **Total Period:** $T = t_{\text{high}} + t_{\text{low}} = 0.693 \times (R_A + 2R_B) \times C$
- **Frequency:** $f = \frac{1.44}{(R_A + 2R_B) \times C}$
- **Duty Cycle:** $D = \frac{R_A + R_B}{R_A + 2R_B} \times 100\%$ (Standard circuit is always $> 50\%$).
ic-ne555.safetyNotes: Standard bipolar NE555 draws a 300mA shoot-through current pulse for ~100ns when switching. Always place a decoupling capacitor right across Pins 1 and 8.

led-5mm.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 5mm LED Quick Reference
- **Color Forward Voltages ($V_f$ at $20\,\text{mA}$):**
  - Red: $\approx 1.8 - 2.0\,\text{V}$
  - Yellow / Orange: $\approx 2.0 - 2.2\,\text{V}$
  - Green: $\approx 2.1 - 2.4\,\text{V}$
  - Blue / Pure White: $\approx 3.0 - 3.4\,\text{V}$
- **Sizing Formula:** $R = \frac{V_{\text{source}} - V_f}{I_f}$
  - For 5V Arduino driving Red LED ($2.0\,\text{V}$, $15\,\text{mA}$): $R = \frac{5 - 2}{0.015} = 200\,\Omega \to$ Use **$220\,\Omega$** standard E12 resistor.
led-5mm.safetyNotes: Never connect an LED to a power source without a current-limiting resistor. The exponential diode I-V curve causes near-infinite current surge at forward threshold.

mcu-atmega328p.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Arduino Uno Hardware Cheat Sheet
- **Pin Current Limits:** Max $20\,\text{mA}$ recommended per pin. Absolute max $40\,\text{mA}$. Total whole-chip limit = $200\,\text{mA}$.
- **Hardware Serial (UART):** Pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX). Connected to USB-to-Serial converter. Avoid using Pins 0 and 1 for general I/O if using `Serial.print()`.
- **Hardware I2C (Two-Wire Interface):** Pin A4 (SDA), Pin A5 (SCL). Standard 100kHz / 400kHz speed. Requires $4.7\,\text{k}\Omega$ pull-ups to 5V.
- **Hardware SPI:** Pin 11 (MOSI), Pin 12 (MISO), Pin 13 (SCK), Pin 10 (SS/CS). High speed synchronous bus (up to 8 MHz).
- **PWM Timer Frequencies:**
  - Pins 5 & 6 (Timer0): $\approx 980\,\text{Hz}$
  - Pins 9 & 10 (Timer1): $\approx 490\,\text{Hz}$
  - Pins 3 & 11 (Timer2): $\approx 490\,\text{Hz}$
mcu-atmega328p.safetyNotes: Power through USB (5V) or 7-12V battery on VIN/barrel jack. Never connect more than 5.5V to any GPIO pin or the 5V rail.

mosfet-irfz44n.name: IRFZ44N N-Channel Power MOSFET
mosfet-irfz44n.package: TO-220AB (Metal tab is connected to Drain)
mosfet-irfz44n.description: High-current N-channel enhancement mode power MOSFET capable of switching up to 49A with ultra-low 17.5mΩ on-resistance (R_DS(on)). Ideal for driving high-power DC motors, heating elements, and solenoid actuators.

pinout.name: Gate (G)
pinout.description: Voltage-controlled input (insulated by SiO2 gate oxide)

pinout.name: Drain (D)
pinout.description: Switched load negative return (internally bonded to metal heatsink tab)

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Drain-Source breakdown V_DSS = 55V. Gate-Source breakdown V_GS = ±20V. Continuous drain current 49A at 25°C with adequate heatsink.

commonMistakes: Driving the gate with 3.3V or 5V logic directly; standard IRFZ44N requires $V_{GS} \ge 10\,\text{V}$ for full conduction! At 5V, it operates in the linear region, causing extreme thermal dissipation and overheating. Use a logic-level MOSFET (e.g. IRLZ44N) or a gate driver for 3.3V/5V MCUs.
Leaving the gate floating without a 10kΩ pull-down resistor; stray static charge will leave the MOSFET partially turned ON.
mosfet-irfz44n.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### IRFZ44N Power MOSFET Quick Reference
- **Pinout (TO-220 front view, metal tab in back):** Pin 1 = Gate, Pin 2 = Drain, Pin 3 = Source. Metal tab = Drain.
- **Gate Pull-Down:** Always connect a $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ resistor from Gate to Source (GND) to guarantee complete shutoff during MCU boot/reset.
- **Gate Resistor:** Place a small $100\,\Omega$ resistor in series with the gate to suppress high-frequency ringing caused by gate capacitance ($C_{iss} \approx 1470\,\text{pF}$).
mosfet-irfz44n.safetyNotes: The metal tab is electrically connected to the Drain pin. If mounting to a shared metal heatsink or robot chassis, use a mica/silicone insulating pad and nylon bushing to prevent shorting.

motor-tt-gearmotor.name: Yellow TT DC Gearmotor (3-6V Dual Shaft)
motor-tt-gearmotor.package: Yellow Plastic Spur Gearbox with Dual Output Shafts
motor-tt-gearmotor.description: Standard hobby robotic propulsion motor pairing a small coreless DC brush motor with an internal 1:48 plastic spur reduction gearbox. Designed for 2WD/4WD wheeled educational mobile robots.

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Rated operating range 3V to 6V DC. Operating at 9V significantly shortens gear tooth and commutator brush lifespan.

commonMistakes: Driving the motor directly from an Arduino digital GPIO pin; pins can only supply 20-40mA, while this motor requires 250mA (and stalls at ~1A), destroying the microcontroller pin instantly! Always use a transistor, MOSFET, or H-bridge driver.
Soldering wires directly to the fragile copper solder tabs without strain relief, breaking the delicate commutator lead terminals.
Omitting noise suppression capacitors (e.g. 100nF ceramic across motor terminals); electrical brush arcing injects massive EMI spikes into nearby sensors and microcontrollers.
motor-tt-gearmotor.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### TT Gearmotor Specifications (at 6V DC)
- **Gear Reduction Ratio:** 1:48
- **No-Load Speed:** $\approx 200 - 240\,\text{RPM}$ (approx $130\,\text{RPM}$ at $3\,\text{V}$)
- **No-Load Current:** $\approx 70\,\text{mA}$
- **Stall Torque:** $\approx 0.8\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{cm}$ ($0.078\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$)
- **Stall Current:** $\approx 800 - 1000\,\text{mA}$
- **EMI Suppression:** Solder one 100nF (0.1µF) ceramic capacitor directly across the two motor terminals to suppress brush arcing noise.
motor-tt-gearmotor.safetyNotes: Safe low-voltage motor (≤ 6V DC). Keep fingers, hair, and clothing clear of rotating wheel shafts and gears.

potentiometer-10k.name: 10kΩ Breadboard Rotary Potentiometer
potentiometer-10k.description: Three-terminal variable resistor functioning as a manual adjustable voltage divider. The center wiper slides along a conductive carbon track between two outer fixed terminals.

pinout.name: Wiper

pinout.name: Terminal 3

commonMistakes: Shorting the wiper: Connecting Terminal 1 to 5V and Wiper to GND turns the wiper into a dead short when rotated to the 5V limit, melting the internal carbon track!

potentiometer-10k.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Potentiometer Quick Reference
- **Voltage Divider Connection:**
  - Pin 1 (Outer): Connect to **+5V**
  - Pin 2 (Center Wiper): Connect to **Arduino Analog Pin (A0)**
  - Pin 3 (Outer): Connect to **GND**
- **Output Equation:** $V_{\text{wiper}} = 5\,\text{V} \times \frac{R_{\text{wiper-to-GND}}}{10\,\text{k}\Omega}$
- **Arduino Analog Read:** `int val = analogRead(A0);` returns an integer from **0 to 1023** ($0\,\text{V}$ to $5.0\,\text{V}$ with 10-bit ADC resolution $\approx 4.88\,\text{mV/step}$).
potentiometer-10k.safetyNotes: Always connect the wiper to a high-impedance input (such as an analog ADC pin or op-amp input). Never draw large currents through the wiper.

regulator-7805.name: L7805 5V 1A Linear Voltage Regulator
regulator-7805.package: TO-220 (Center pin and metal tab are Ground)
regulator-7805.description: Fixed 5V positive linear voltage regulator providing up to 1.0A output with internal current limiting and thermal shutdown protection. Essential for stepping down 7-12V battery packs to a clean 5V logic rail.

pinout.name: GROUND (GND)

commonMistakes: Forgetting that linear regulators dissipate all excess voltage as heat: Ploss = (Vin - 5V) * I. Feeding 12V at 500mA causes 3.5W of heat dissipation, burning fingers without a heatsink!

regulator-7805.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 7805 Regulator Quick Reference
- **Pinout (TO-220 front view with metal tab in back):** Pin 1 = Input (Vin), Pin 2 = Ground (GND), Pin 3 = Output (+5V).
- **Capacitor Sizing:** Place a $0.33\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor on Pin 1 (Input to GND) and a $0.1\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor on Pin 3 (Output to GND).

regulator-7805.safetyNotes: The metal tab is Ground (0V), making it safe to attach to grounded metal heatsinks. The heatsink may become very hot under heavy loads (> 60°C).

resistor-axial.name: Resistor (1/4W Through-Hole)
resistor-axial.description: Two-terminal linear passive component that implements electrical resistance, dropping voltage and limiting current according to Ohm's Law.

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Rated at 0.25W (250 mW) continuous at 70°C ambient. Derate power linearly above 70°C.

commonMistakes: Using a 1/4W resistor for high-current loads (e.g. directly in series with high power motors), causing thermal discoloration and burnout.
Misreading multiplier color bands (e.g. mistaking 10kΩ for 1kΩ or 100Ω).
Ignoring tolerance (5% gold band vs 1% brown band) in precision analog sensing dividers.
resistor-axial.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Resistor Quick Reference
- **Ohm's Law:** $V = I \times R$, $I = V / R$, $R = V / I$
- **Power Dissipation:** $P = V \times I = I^2 \times R = V^2 / R$
- **Series Resistance:** $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$
- **Parallel Resistance:** $1/R_{eq} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + \dots$
- **Color Code (4-band):** Band 1 = 1st digit, Band 2 = 2nd digit, Band 3 = multiplier ($10^x$), Band 4 = tolerance (Gold = ±5%, Brown = ±1%).
resistor-axial.safetyNotes: Always calculate expected power dissipation ($P = I^2 R$). Ensure operating power is $\le 50\%$ of rated wattage (125 mW for 1/4W resistors) for safety headroom.

sensor-dht11.name: DHT11 Digital Temperature & Humidity Sensor
sensor-dht11.package: 4-Pin Single In-Line (or 3-Pin Breadboard Module with Built-in Pull-Up)
sensor-dht11.description: Basic, ultra low-cost digital composite sensor containing a resistive humidity measurement component, an NTC temperature sensor, and an 8-bit microcontroller outputting single-wire serialized digital data.

pinout.name: DATA
pinout.description: Bi-directional single-bus serialized digital data pin

pinout.name: NC
pinout.description: Not connected (present on 4-pin bare packages, omitted on 3-pin modules)

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Humidity measurement range: 20-90% RH (±5% accuracy). Temperature range: 0-50°C (±2°C accuracy).

commonMistakes: Reading the sensor faster than once every 1 to 2 seconds; sensor takes up to 1 second to update internal humidity registers, returning duplicate or corrupted checksum frames.
Omitting the 4.7kΩ - 10kΩ pull-up resistor from the DATA line to VCC on 4-pin bare packages.
sensor-dht11.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### DHT11 Single-Bus Protocol Reference
- **Pull-Up Resistor:** Connect a $4.7\,\text{k}\Omega$ to $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ resistor between Pin 2 (DATA) and Pin 1 (VCC) if using a 4-pin bare package (3-pin PCB modules typically have this pre-soldered).
- **40-Bit Data Frame Structure:**
  - Byte 1: Humidity Integer (8 bits)
  - Byte 2: Humidity Decimal (8 bits, 0 for DHT11)
  - Byte 3: Temperature Integer (8 bits)
  - Byte 4: Temperature Decimal (8 bits, 0 for DHT11)
  - Byte 5: Checksum = Byte 1 + Byte 2 + Byte 3 + Byte 4 (lowest 8 bits)
- **Sampling Rate:** Minimum interval between reads is **1.0 second**.
sensor-dht11.safetyNotes: Operates on safe low voltages (3.3V to 5V). Do not expose sensor to condensed water or direct rain.

servo-sg90.description: Compact 180-degree position-controlled actuator integrating a coreless DC motor, nylon gearbox, feedback potentiometer, and closed-loop error amplifier in a 9g chassis. Controlled by 50Hz PWM pulse width.

Always power servos from an external 5-6V battery pack or regulator with shared ground!
Forcing the horn past 0° or 180° by hand; strips the miniature nylon gear teeth.
servo-sg90.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### SG90 Servo Timing Quick Reference
- **Frame Rate:** Standard 50 Hz PWM ($20\,\text{ms}$ repeat frame).
- **Pulse Width Mapping:**
  - $\approx 544\,\mu\text{s} \to$ **0°** (Full clockwise)
  - $\approx 1500\,\mu\text{s} \to$ **90°** (Center / Neutral)
  - $\approx 2400\,\mu\text{s} \to$ **180°** (Full counter-clockwise)
- **Arduino Code Snippet:**
  ```cpp
  #include <Servo.h>
  Servo myServo;
  void setup() {
    myServo.attach(9); // Signal on Pin 9
    myServo.write(90); // Move to 90 degrees
  }
  ```
servo-sg90.safetyNotes: Power servos from an external 5V power supply or battery pack. Connect the battery negative terminal to the Arduino GND pin (common ground reference).

switch-tactile-6mm.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### Tactile Switch Wiring Best Practice
- **Internal Connection Rule:** Pins on the same long side are permanently bridged inside the plastic housing. The switch only closes the circuit between opposite sides when pressed down.
- **Recommended Arduino Wiring (Active LOW):**
  - Connect one side of the button to an Arduino digital pin (e.g. Pin 2).
  - Connect the opposite side directly to **GND**.
  - In Arduino C++, enable the internal pull-up resistor: `pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);`.
  - Reading logic: `digitalRead(2) == LOW` means the button is **pressed**. No external resistor required!

transistor-2n2222.name: 2N2222 / PN2222 NPN Bipolar Junction Transistor
transistor-2n2222.package: TO-92 Plastic (Flat side facing front: E-B-C)
transistor-2n2222.description: Ubiquitous NPN bipolar junction transistor for low-side switching and linear amplification. Controlled by small base current to switch larger collector-emitter currents.

pinout.name: Emitter (E)
pinout.description: Connected to circuit ground in low-side switch

pinout.name: Base (B)
pinout.description: Control terminal, requires a current-limiting series resistor

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Collector-Emitter breakdown V_CEO = 40V. Maximum continuous collector current I_C = 800 mA.

commonMistakes: Connecting microcontroller GPIO directly to Base pin without a series base resistor; forward biased B-E diode ($V_{BE} \approx 0.7V$) creates a short on the GPIO pin!
Swapping Emitter and Collector pins due to differing TO-18 (metal can) vs TO-92 (plastic) pinouts.
transistor-2n2222.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 2N2222 NPN Switch Quick Reference
- **Pinout (TO-92 flat face facing you):** Pin 1 = Emitter, Pin 2 = Base, Pin 3 = Collector.
- **Saturation Rule (Full ON):** To ensure hard saturation ($V_{CE} \approx 0.1 - 0.2\,\text{V}$), provide base overdrive ratio $I_B \approx I_C / 10$ to $I_C / 20$.
- **Base Resistor Sizing:** $R_B = \frac{V_{\text{GPIO}} - 0.7\,\text{V}}{I_B}$.
  - Example for 5V Arduino switching 100mA relay ($I_B = 5\,\text{mA}$): $R_B = \frac{5 - 0.7}{0.005} = 860\,\Omega \to$ Use **$1\,\text{k}\Omega$**.
transistor-2n2222.safetyNotes: Always include a base resistor ($1\,\text{k}\Omega$ typical) to protect microcontroller output pins from overcurrent. When switching inductive loads (motors/relays), always install a flyback diode.

transistor-2n3906.name: 2N3906 PNP Bipolar Junction Transistor
transistor-2n3906.package: TO-92 Plastic (Flat side facing front: E-B-C)
transistor-2n3906.description: Standard PNP bipolar junction transistor for high-side switching and complementary push-pull driver stages. Turns ON when base is pulled lower than emitter by 0.7V.

pinout.name: Emitter (E)
pinout.description: Connected to positive supply rail in high-side switch

pinout.name: Base (B)
pinout.description: Control terminal, pulled LOW to ground to activate

absoluteMaxRatings.notes: Collector-Emitter breakdown V_CEO = -40V. Maximum continuous collector current I_C = 200 mA.

commonMistakes: Attempting to switch a 12V supply with a 5V microcontroller directly; when GPIO is HIGH (5V), $V_{EB} = 12 - 5 = 7\,\text{V}$, leaving the transistor permanently turned ON and potentially back-powering the 5V MCU!
Omitting base pull-up resistor to positive rail to keep switch reliably OFF during boot.
transistor-2n3906.cheatSheetMarkdown:
### 2N3906 PNP High-Side Quick Reference
- **Pinout (TO-92 flat face facing you):** Pin 1 = Emitter (to VCC), Pin 2 = Base (control via resistor), Pin 3 = Collector (out to load).
- **Switching Logic:**
  - Base pulled to $V_{\text{emitter}}$ ($V_{BE} = 0\,\text{V}$) $\to$ **OFF** (open circuit).
  - Base pulled LOW ($V_B \le V_{\text{emitter}} - 0.7\,\text{V}$) $\to$ **ON** (current conducts from Emitter to Collector).
transistor-2n3906.safetyNotes: If supply rail voltage is higher than MCU GPIO voltage, use an intermediate NPN transistor to pull the PNP base down safely.

p1-led-blink-lab.title: LED Blink & Timing Lab
p1-led-blink-lab.description: Build your first physical circuit on a breadboard and control an LED with precise millisecond timing code on the Arduino Uno.
verifyChecklist: Verify 220 ohm resistor maintains LED current below 20mA
Verify standard 5mm red LED forward voltage is approximately 1.8V to 2.0V
Confirm Arduino Uno pin 13 delivers 5V digital HIGH
safetyRules: Always disconnect the USB cable before placing or moving wires on the breadboard.
Never connect an LED directly across 5V and GND without a series resistor; doing so causes excess current and permanently burns out the LED.
Operate exclusively from 5V USB bus power. Do not connect mains power or external battery packs for this basic circuit.

bom.spec: ATmega328P DIP or SMD development board with USB-B cable
bom.notes: Any 5V ATmega328P board will work identically.

bom.name: 5mm Diffused LED (Red)
bom.notes: Longer lead is the positive anode (+); shorter lead and flat flat edge is the cathode (-).

bom.notes: Resistors have no polarity; either orientation is fine.

bom.notes: Columns 1 to 30 share internal 5-hole vertical clips.
